title: Rick Riordan as a Myth Adapter

objectives.text: Students will determine what an author believes about myths by analyzing word choice in an interview excerpt.
Students will use the comparison structures *while*, *whereas*, *unlike* and *both…and* to explain how a myth changes when it is retold.
Students will use the affixes *trans-* and *-tion* to determine the meaning of **transform** and **modernization**.

essentialQuestions: How do myths reflect cultural values?
How do retellings change across cultures and generations?

connections.knowledgeBuilding: Students learn how an author decides what to keep and what to change when he retells an ancient story for modern readers.
connections.enduringUnderstanding: Retellings keep a story alive by connecting old ideas to a new audience.
connections.futureLessons: Tonight students begin *The Lightning Thief*, Chapter 1, and will look for the first signs of Riordan's choices.
connections.performanceTask: The comparison language introduced today is the grammar of the culminating explanatory essay.

texts.title: "I'm hardly the first to modernise Greek myths" (interview excerpt)
texts.author: Rick Riordan

sections.title: Launch
sections.purpose: Activate what students already know about myths and hook them on the idea of an old story set in New York City.

activities.title: Turn and Talk: Monsters in Manhattan

blocks.text: Imagine a Greek god living in an apartment in New York City. What would he do for work? What would make him angry?
With your partner, take one minute each to describe a god or monster you know and how it might show up in a modern city.
Medusa could run a garden-statue shop, because anyone who looks at her turns to stone.
Listen for two or three playful answers to share aloud. Do not correct mythological details yet.
Today we will read what Rick Riordan says about doing exactly this, and we will look closely at the **words** he uses to explain why.

sections.title: Learning in Action
sections.purpose: Analyze how Riordan's word choice reveals what he believes myths do for readers.

blocks.text: Writers choose words on purpose. When Riordan calls himself an *adapter*, the suffix *-er* tells us he is a person who adapts. Let's find other words that show what he does to old stories.
Read the interview excerpt. Underline words Riordan uses to describe changing a myth, and write a question mark next to one word you would like to understand better.
What does the word *transform* suggest about how much Riordan changes a myth?
It suggests he changes a lot, not just small details, because transform means to change completely.

blocks.stem: The prefix *trans-* means "across" or "change." Which meaning of **transform** fits Riordan's interview?

choices.rationale: Copying keeps a story the same; *trans-* signals change.

choices.text: to change a story into a new form
choices.rationale: *Trans-* plus *form* means to change the form of something, which is what an adapter does.

choices.text: to translate a story into Greek
choices.rationale: Translation is one kind of change, but Riordan writes in English for modern readers.

blocks.purpose: Language focus: using word parts to unlock meaning. Before reading, preview *trans-*, *-tion* and *-er* with one familiar example each.
blocks.sayAsk: Use the frame: "The word ___ has the part ___, which means ___, so the word means ___." Students may discuss in their home language first, then share in English.
blocks.watchFor: If students guess meanings from the whole word only → Prompt: "Cover the prefix. What word is left?" Success: students explain one word using its parts.

activities.title: Part B: Old Story, New City

blocks.text: Think about one way Riordan says he modernizes myths. Then compare it with the original myth using *while*, *whereas*, *unlike* or *both…and*.
Sentence frame: *While* the ancient myth ___, Riordan's version ___.
While the ancient myth takes place on Mount Olympus, Riordan's version puts Olympus above the Empire State Building.

rows.situation: Struggling with: finding a change to compare
rows.tryThis: Point to the interview line about setting and ask, "Where did the old story happen? Where does his happen?"
Ask students to explain *why* Riordan might make that change for readers today.

sections.title: Look Back
sections.purpose: Students explain in writing what Riordan believes myths do for people.

blocks.text: In two or three sentences, explain one word Riordan uses that shows what he believes myths do for readers.
Read and annotate *The Lightning Thief* Chapter 1 (pp. 1–8). Mark one place where something ancient appears in the modern world.
